content: The untethered regimen is a method that integrates the use of an insulin pump with a long-acting insulin analog, such as Lantus or Levemir. This approach allows individuals who are dependent on insulin to disconnect from their pump when desired while still benefiting from the flexibility and control that the pump provides. The term untethered regimen was introduced by Dr. Steve Edelman, an endocrinologist and type 1 diabetic who uses an insulin pump himself. Dr. Edelman advocates for diabetes management plans that are personalized to each individual, enabling optimal diabetes care outcomes while maintaining a fulfilling lifestyle. Dr. Edelman developed this technique because he wanted the freedom to remove his insulin pump for extended periods, such as during swimming or sports activities, sometimes for an entire weekend. This method provides the advantage of being free from the constant attachment to the pump while still maintaining effective blood glucose control. Removing the Pump Sports and Exercise The intensity and duration of physical activity often influence how insulin pump users manage their basal insulin delivery. Many users employ a temporary basal rate to reduce the amount of insulin delivered during exercise, as physical activity typically decreases the body's insulin requirements. The appropriate reduction is determined through trial and error, with regular blood glucose monitoring. Some users may suspend the basal rate entirely or disconnect the pump during exercise. In certain cases, individuals may choose to keep the pump on during sports to allow for real-time adjustments in insulin delivery. This involves reducing the pump's basal rate. Alternatively, some users prefer to remove the pump altogether. In such scenarios, a combination of long-acting insulin (e.g., Lantus or Levemir) and the pump's basal rate can work synergistically. The pump can be removed before planned activities, such as football practice, water skiing, or dancing, while the long-acting insulin maintains a reduced basal insulin level. Once the activity is completed, the pump can be reconnected. Water Activities Although some insulin pumps are waterproof, their high cost often makes users cautious about exposing them to water. Pumps can typically be disconnected for short periods, such as during bathing, without significant issues. However, for activities like hot tub parties or a day at the beach, removing the pump and adopting the untethered regimen can provide a welcome break. Different water sports impose varying demands on the individual. For example, sailing may involve long dry periods interrupted by occasional wet conditions, while swimming laps for an hour each morning is a consistent aerobic activity. On the other hand, a toddler playing in a shallow pool may experience the most intense workout of all. Each situation requires the pump user to learn how to adjust their basal insulin delivery, especially when combining a portion of the basal insulin with long-acting insulin. This allows the pump to be removed for extended periods while maintaining adequate blood glucose control. To regularly enjoy water sports, pump users collaborate with their diabetes care team to develop a tailored plan. Pump Vacations Dr. Edelman initially developed the untethered regimen because he wanted to remove his pump for the weekend. During weekdays, he uses his insulin pump to benefit from its flexibility. In this case, he administers Lantus to cover three-quarters of his total basal insulin needs and uses the pump to deliver the remaining one-quarter. This setup allows for temporary adjustments to the pump's basal rate as needed. On Friday nights, when he typically administers his daily Lantus injection, he doses for 100% of his basal insulin needs and removes the pump for the weekend. During this time, he uses an insulin pen for food and correction boluses as needed. Alternatively, the pump can be reconnected to the quick-disconnect site on the infusion set if required. On Sunday nights, at the time of his Lantus injection, Dr. Edelman doses for three-quarters of his basal needs with Lantus and reconnects the pump. Occasionally, an insulin pump may require repair. Pump manufacturers usually provide quick turnaround times, and replacement pumps are sent promptly. During such times, individuals may need to manage without the pump for a few days. Familiarity with the untethered regimen can be beneficial in these situations. Insurance Against Ketoacidosis All individuals dependent on insulin are at risk of developing diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) if insulin delivery is interrupted for a prolonged period. The time it takes for DKA to develop varies depending on the individual and their circumstances. For example, an undetected pump issue at night—such as running out of insulin, a dead battery, or a leaking infusion set—can lead to DKA by morning. Using long-acting insulin, such as Lantus or Levemir, to cover a significant portion of basal insulin needs can provide a safety net. The pump's basal rate program can then be used to supplement the remaining insulin requirements. Administering Lantus once daily serves as a backup for pump users and can be particularly advantageous for those who are prone to developing DKA quickly.
